input:
## Current use

This energy assessment provides a comprehensive overview of energy use at a dairy plant, with a particular focus on electricity consumption and on the opportunities that may exist to improve the overall energy position of the site. Electricity use at the plant is 3617 MWh per year, and this annual figure forms the central reference point for the assessment as a whole. Within that total, refrigeration takes the largest share of electricity use, which means that refrigeration is not simply one load among many but is instead the dominant element in the site's electricity profile. This is an important point, because it helps to explain why the assessment gives particular attention to refrigeration and to the possibilities for recovering heat from the refrigeration system. At the same time, it is worth noting that an annual electricity total of this kind brings together a wide range of operating patterns across the year. Production schedules change, storage requirements vary, and the demands placed on the plant are not constant from week to week or from season to season. The annual figure is therefore best understood as an aggregate picture of electricity use rather than as a description of any single operating day. Nevertheless, it provides a clear and useful basis for the assessment, and the prominence of refrigeration within the total is a consistent theme that runs through the sections that follow.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration occupies a central position in the energy profile of the dairy plant, both because it takes the largest share of electricity use and because it operates in support of activities that are fundamental to the functioning of the site. The refrigeration system has to maintain appropriate conditions for materials and products that depend on reliable cooling, and it has to do so in a dependable manner across the full range of operating circumstances that the plant experiences. Loads on the system arise from the products that are cooled and stored, from heat entering cooled spaces, from the operation of associated equipment, and from the general movement of people and materials around the site. For these reasons, refrigeration demand is not a single fixed quantity but a changing load that responds to production activity and to the way in which cooled spaces are used and managed. Good operational practice therefore has an important role to play. Careful attention to the use of cooled storage, prompt attention to maintenance needs, and disciplined management of the openings through which heat can enter cooled areas all contribute to keeping the refrigeration load as low as reasonably practicable. At the same time, refrigeration is also the source of the heat that the proposed retrofit seeks to recover. In the course of its operation, the refrigeration system rejects heat, and it is this rejected heat that creates the opportunity for heat recovery. Any heat-recovery arrangement nevertheless has to respect the primary purpose of the refrigeration system. Cooling performance cannot be compromised in the pursuit of recovered heat, and the recovery arrangement needs to work alongside the refrigeration duty rather than in competition with it. It is within this context that the retrofit proposal should be understood.

## Steam

Steam forms the other major element of the energy picture considered in this assessment, although the evidence available in relation to steam is considerably less complete than the evidence available in relation to electricity. The steam figures used in the assessment are from one winter month. This is an important qualification, because a single month cannot be expected to represent the pattern of steam use across a whole year, and a winter month in particular may reflect seasonal conditions that differ markedly from those experienced at other times. Steam use at the plant is associated with the heating duties that arise in the course of production and with the general services that support operation. As with refrigeration, the load is not constant, and it varies with the level and pattern of activity on the site. Distribution and standby losses also form part of the overall picture, since steam systems characteristically lose energy between the point at which steam is raised and the points at which it is used. Because the available figures rest on one winter month, the assessment treats the steam position with appropriate caution. The figures are used to indicate the presence and general character of steam demand rather than to support detailed annual conclusions. This seasonal limitation is flagged again in the recommendation, where it is important that decisions are not based on steam figures that may give a misleading impression of the year as a whole. The steam section should therefore be read as a qualified part of the assessment, in contrast to the electricity position, which rests on a full annual figure.

## Recommendation

The recommendation of this assessment is that the heat-recovery retrofit should be taken forward, on the basis of the electricity case set out in the preceding sections. The retrofit is projected to save 20% of electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 723 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $498k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $86,808, and the derived simple payback is 5.7 years. These figures indicate that the project offers a worthwhile financial return on the basis of the electricity savings alone, while also reducing the overall energy demand of the site. It is recommended that site management should now progress the retrofit to the next stage of development, including confirmation that the recovered heat can be used effectively within the plant and that the arrangement can be integrated with the refrigeration system without compromising cooling performance. It is also recommended that the steam figures should not be used as part of the financial case at this stage, because those figures are drawn from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal. Overall, the assessment supports a positive decision on the retrofit, founded on the measured annual electricity position and on the central role of refrigeration within it, with the steam position to be revisited when a fuller picture of steam use across the year is available. Taken as a whole, the assessment is intended to give decision-makers a balanced and evidence-based picture: a clear account of where electricity is used, a careful explanation of the role played by refrigeration, a suitably cautious treatment of the steam position, and a recommendation that follows from the strongest parts of the evidence. The structure of the document reflects that intention, and each section contributes to the overall conclusion that the proposed retrofit merits further development.

## Current use

Electricity is the firmly based part of this assessment, and refrigeration dominates it. Electricity use at the dairy plant is 3617 MWh per year. Refrigeration takes the largest share of that total. The retrofit case in the recommendation rests on those two statements: an annual electricity figure that is measured, and a load structure in which the largest single use is the system whose rejected heat the retrofit would recover. The annual total aggregates a year of varying production and storage activity. It is not a description of any single day, and it should not be used as one. Its role is to fix the scale of electricity use and the share structure within it. On that role it is sufficient. Steam stands on weaker evidence, as the steam section sets out, and no part of the financial case in the recommendation is built on steam. The assessment therefore separates its conclusions by the quality of their bases. Conclusions about electricity and refrigeration rest on the annual figure. Conclusions about steam are held at the level the evidence supports, which is qualitative. That separation governs the recommendation: the retrofit is appraised on electricity alone, and the steam position is recorded as an open item rather than absorbed into the case as if it were measured. A further feature of the annual figure is that it conceals the timing of use. Electricity taken by refrigeration during production peaks and electricity taken to hold storage conditions overnight enter the same total, although they arise from different activities and respond to different controls. The assessment does not separate them, because the retrofit case does not require the separation: the case turns on the annual quantity and on refrigeration's share of it. Where a later design stage needs the load profile, metering at the refrigeration system will have to supply it.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration takes the largest share of electricity use because cooling at the plant is continuous, load-bearing work. Cooled materials and products depend on the system holding its conditions through production, storage and movement across the site. The load itself is composite. Product entering cooled space brings heat with it. Cooled rooms gain heat through their fabric and through their doors. Fans, pumps and other associated equipment add their own heat to the spaces they serve. Production activity sets the overall level, and the pattern of the working day sets its variation. Operational discipline acts on several of these components at once: doors kept closed limit heat entry, maintained heat-exchange surfaces keep the plant working at its intended duty, and set-points held at their specified values prevent the system from cooling beyond the requirement. None of that changes the structural point. Refrigeration is the site's largest electricity use and the source of a continuous rejected-heat stream. The retrofit addresses the second of those facts. It would recover heat that the refrigeration system must reject in any case. The governing condition is that recovery stays subordinate to cooling. A heat-recovery arrangement that raised the refrigeration system's condensing burden or disturbed its control would trade the plant's primary duty for a secondary gain, and the assessment does not support such an arrangement. Recovery must take the heat the system rejects under its normal operation, at conditions the system already produces. The load structure also explains why refrigeration is treated as the assessment's centre rather than as one item in a list of uses. A saving applied to the largest share acts on the largest base. Measures addressed to smaller uses may still be worth taking, but they cannot carry a site-level case of this size, and the assessment accordingly spends its detail where the electricity is.

## Steam

Steam figures in this assessment are from one winter month, and they are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation. That single qualification controls everything that can be said about steam here. A winter month shows steam demand under winter conditions: heating duties at their seasonal level, distribution losses under the corresponding load, and production at whatever level that month carried. It does not show the annual pattern. Annualising one winter month would build the seasonal peak into every month of the year and would overstate the steam position by an amount that cannot be estimated from the month itself. The assessment therefore makes no annual claim for steam. Steam is recorded as a present and material energy use, associated with the heating duties of production and with site services, and its distribution and standby losses are noted as part of that use. No quantity is attached to any of those statements, because the evidence does not carry one. This is a deliberate asymmetry in the assessment. Electricity has an annual measured figure and is used quantitatively. Steam has a single seasonal month and is used qualitatively. When a full year of steam figures is available, the steam position can be restated on the same basis as electricity and the assessment can be extended. Until then, the seasonal flag is not a defect in the assessment; it is the assessment's accurate statement of what the steam evidence is. The same caution applies to comparisons with other sites. Steam use depends on the products made, the heating duties they impose and the season in which the figures were taken. A winter month from this plant cannot be set against an annual figure from another plant, or against this plant's own annual electricity figure, without misstating both. The figures are kept in their own frame: one month, in winter, at this site.

## Recommendation

Site management should take the heat-recovery retrofit forward on the electricity case. The retrofit is projected to save 20% of electricity use, a derived saving of 723 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $498k. At $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $86,808 and the derived simple payback is 5.7 years. The case is complete without steam: the projected saving is a share of a measured annual figure, the price is stated, and the payback follows from the two. Three conditions attach to the recommendation. The recovered heat must have a use on site that can accept it at the conditions the refrigeration system produces. The recovery arrangement must leave refrigeration performance and control undisturbed, for the reason given in the refrigeration section. Post-installation metering must record the electricity saving so that the projected figure is replaced by a measured one. The steam figures are excluded from the financial case. They are from one winter month, they are seasonal, and including them would weaken a case that does not need them. The decision requested is approval to develop the retrofit on the electricity basis stated, with the steam assessment to be revisited when a full year of steam figures exists. Development of the retrofit should also fix the measurement boundary before installation. The projected saving is a share of site electricity use, attributed to the refrigeration system. Unless the refrigeration load is metered separately, the saving will be visible only as a change in the site total, where production variation can mask it. A metered boundary at the refrigeration system converts the post-installation check from an argument about the site total into a direct reading of the load the retrofit acts on.
